Need to search first.Let me try a few more searches to fill gaps.I've compiled notes on Isaiah 45 below, but they're incomplete. My tools only returned search-result excerpts and every attempt to open a full page failed, so several verses are thin. I wrote nothing for verse 16 because I found no comment on it. There are no Lutheran, Pentecostal, Wesleyan-Methodist, Orthodox, modern-scholarship (netbible, bibleodyssey) or prosperity-teaching points, because none of those sources came up.

**How to read the URLs:** pages like biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/45-N.htm collect many older commentators on one page. Where the excerpt didn't show which commentator wrote a remark, I say "a commentator on this page" instead of guessing.

---

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1:**
- Ellicott says "anointed" (*mashiach*, the Hebrew word behind "Messiah") is the same title the Bible gives Saul, David's line and even Abraham. Calling Cyrus this means he would be king "by the grace of God" as truly as David was. "Loose the loins" means to ungird or disarm, since swords hung from the belt. The gates may hint at Babylon's famous brazen gates, the "hundred brazen gates" in Herodotus. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/45.htm
- Commentators on this page agree that no oil was poured on Cyrus. He is called "anointed" because God set him apart and equipped him for a task. One adds that this doesn't prove Cyrus was godly or worshipped the true God. Another notes that the gates leading to the river were left open the night Cyrus marched his army up the emptied channel into Babylon. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/45-1.htm
- Ligonier notes that Cyrus wasn't a son of David, so he isn't the promised Messiah of Isaiah 9 and 11. It quotes Calvin: the title wasn't permanent, but was given because Cyrus "for a time" did a redeemer's work for the church. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/cyrus-lords-anointed
- Matthew Henry sees Cyrus as a type, or picture, of the coming Redeemer. He reads God holding Cyrus's right hand as God both strengthening and directing him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_045.cfm

**v. 2:**
- Ellicott renders the phrase "make the dwelling-places smooth," meaning God removes every obstacle. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/45.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary prefers "make the rugged places level," meaning God smooths Cyrus's way. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/45.htm

**v. 3:**
- Ellicott takes the "treasures of darkness" to be Babylon's piled-up wealth. He adds that taking Sardis, with the riches of Croesus, brought similar plunder. Cyrus was meant to see in his victories the hand of Israel's God protecting him, and so accept his role as the deliverer of God's people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/45.htm

**v. 4:**
- Ellicott says "servant" and "elect" point to the ideal, true Israel (the true church) more than the outward nation, so world history is arranged for the sake of God's true people. "Called thee by thy name" may mean predicting Cyrus's actual name, or giving him titles like "anointed" and "shepherd." "Though thou hast not known me" may mean before Cyrus acknowledged God (Ezra 1), or even before he was born. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/45.htm
- David Guzik notes that Cyrus didn't know the LORD, yet God still anointed and used him. Guzik adds that Cyrus "apparently listened," and cites an ancient claim that Cyrus read Isaiah's prophecy about himself. https://blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/studyguide_isa/isa_45.cfm
- Matthew Henry says God's favour to Cyrus wasn't for Cyrus's own sake, and whether Cyrus was a virtuous man "is questioned." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_045.cfm

**v. 5:**
- Ellicott says "no God beside me" normally answers polytheism (belief in many gods). Here it may be aimed at Persian dualism, the belief in two rival gods of good and evil. "I girded thee" is the reverse of verse 1's "ungirding": God gives Cyrus strength. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/45.htm
- A commentator on this page (seemingly Keil and Delitzsch) holds that the repeated "though thou hast not known me" means before Cyrus even existed, not while he still worshipped idols. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/45-5.htm
- Matthew Henry hears God telling Cyrus that his own idol didn't equip him; the God he didn't know did. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_045.cfm

**v. 6:**
- GotQuestions says Cyrus would be God's instrument for spreading word of God's righteousness and salvation "from east to west." https://www.gotquestions.org/Isaiah-45-7.html
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary says a key aim of this whole episode was to free Cyrus and his people from belief in two eternal principles, Light and Darkness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/isaiah-45.html

**v. 7:**
The commentators broadly agree on this verse.
- Ellicott says the verse doesn't address where evil came from. "Evil" here, set against "peace," means suffering, not sin. Such suffering is usually both the result of moral evil and God's correction of it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/45.htm
- This page collects several voices. Benson quotes Bishop Lowth that the verse answers the Persian Magian (priestly) belief in two independent causes of good and evil. Matthew Henry's Concise Commentary says it means the evil of punishment, not of sin. Barnes says "darkness" and "evil" don't refer to sin. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says "evil" here means war or disaster (compare Amos 3:6). Gill cites the Jewish teachers Kimchi and Saadiah, who read the verse against belief in two gods. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/45-7.htm
- GotQuestions says the Hebrew *ra'* can mean moral evil or calamity, and here it means calamity, as most modern translations show. God doesn't create moral evil, but as ruler he can bring disaster, as he did on Babylon through Cyrus. https://www.gotquestions.org/Isaiah-45-7.html
- This page gathers several more. Coffman, citing Kidner, says *ra'* is too general a word to make God the author of wickedness. Chuck Smith calls "evil" an unfortunate translation. Constable says God isn't claiming to create moral evil but well-being (*shalom*) and calamity. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/45-7.html

**v. 8:**
- Ellicott sees a vision of a new heaven and new earth, with righteousness falling like rain from above and growing up from the ground. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/45.htm

**v. 9:**
- Ellicott thinks the people "quarrelling" are probably Israelites who wanted a different deliverer, such as a prince of David's line. "A potsherd among potsherds" means a frail mortal like everyone else. The point, as in Jeremiah 18 and Romans 9, is God's absolute sovereignty. The first question challenges God; the second ("He has no hands") scornfully condemns him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/45.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary says Isaiah expects Israel to grumble that their deliverer is a pagan king, not one of their own. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/45.htm
- The Bible Hub study notes say God owes no one an explanation. The verse calls us back to humble trust in the skilful Potter. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/45-9.htm

**v. 10:**
- Ellicott: people accept the circumstances of their birth without blaming their parents, so how much more should they accept what God arranges for nations and individuals. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/45.htm

**v. 11:**
- Ellicott: as printed, the verse invites people to ask the Holy One about the future rather than pagan oracles. A slight change to the Hebrew text gives "Will ye question me … command me?", which is what the grumblers were in effect doing. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/45.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary reads it as: first learn God's plans, then, if you must, give him directions about his sons. Don't presume to instruct him while ignorant of his designs. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/45.htm

**v. 12:**
- Ellicott: the Creator is also the Ruler, supreme in history as in nature. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/45.htm

**v. 13:**
- Ellicott calls this God's answer to the grumblers. The rebuilt city and returned exiles would show that God's righteousness directed Cyrus. Cyrus would act not from greed but because the Lord stirred his spirit (2 Chronicles 36:22). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/45.htm
- Matthew Henry notes the captives are freed without ransom. He applies this to Christ, anointed to open the prison for captive souls (Isaiah 61:1). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_045.cfm

**v. 14:**
- Ellicott says a new section begins. Egypt, Cush and Seba now come freely, as converts to Israel's faith, in bondage they choose for themselves. A partial fulfilment may be Cyrus ordering other nations to help rebuild the Temple (Ezra 1:4). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/45.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary describes the "hardworking" Egyptians and the "trade-loving" Ethiopians and Sabeans. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/45.htm

**v. 15:**
- Ellicott gives two readings: the nations' words of wonder continue, or the prophet himself marvels at God's unsearchable ways (Romans 11:33). During the exile God seemed hidden, but he had been working all along. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/45.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary prefers the first reading. The converted nations marvel that God hid himself so long and has now shown himself through Cyrus. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/45.htm
- Commentators on this page say God sometimes hides his face from his people, so they must wait patiently through suffering. A sermon on the page (it reads like MacLaren) insists that despite all mystery, God has revealed enough. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/45-15.htm

**v. 17:**
- Ellicott: "world without end" literally means "for the ages." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/45.htm

**v. 18:**
- Commentators on this page say God didn't make the earth to remain an empty wilderness. One applies this to Judah, which would be peopled again after the exile. Gill notes that the Hebrew word here is *tohu*, the word for the "formless" earth in Genesis 1:2, but the earth wasn't created to stay that way. The Geneva notes say it was formed to be inhabited by people, "but chiefly of his Church." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/45-18.htm
- Calvin says this extends to all humanity: God feeds even the wicked because he decreed that people should live on the earth. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/45-18.html

**v. 19:**
- A sermon on this page (seemingly MacLaren) contrasts verses 15 and 19. Whatever is obscure, God's revelation itself isn't. He is found by those who seek him and is "no hidden God" lurking in obscurity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/45-15.htm

**v. 20:**
- Ellicott: "you fugitives from the nations" are mainly survivors of Cyrus's conquests who now acknowledge Israel's God and can testify that idols are worthless. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-45.html

**v. 21:**
- A commentator on this page (seemingly Barnes): God being both just and merciful is the ground for confidence in looking to him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/45-22.htm

**v. 22:**
- The Pulpit Commentary reads "look" as "turn," meaning be converted. It says this implies all can turn if they will, and salvation follows. Another commentator calls it "the look of conversion." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/45-22.htm
- Spurgeon says the verse shows God alone saves: look to him, not to a priest or to yourself. The way is simple, "Look," and it is offered to "the ends of the earth," meaning the worst of sinners. https://www.spurgeon.org/resource-library/sermons/sovereignty-and-salvation/
- Constable: because God alone saves, salvation is offered to all nations, not just Israel. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/45-22.html
- Spurgeon was converted through this text in 1850. A lay Primitive Methodist preacher told the congregation to stop looking to themselves and look to Christ. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/blogs/justin-taylor/charles-spurgeons-conversion-in-a-primitive-methodist-chapel/ ; also https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-45/

**v. 23:**
- Commentators on this page call swearing by himself God's most solemn possible oath (Hebrews 6:13). Bowing the knee and swearing by God's name mean worship and submission by all nations. Ellicott notes Paul applies the verse to Christ (Philippians 2:10; Romans 14:11). The Geneva notes say faith must be confessed outwardly, not only held in the heart. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/45-23.htm
- Precept Austin points out that in Isaiah the knees bow to Yahweh (the LORD), and Paul applies this to Jesus. https://www.preceptaustin.org/philippians_210_commentary
- GotQuestions sees Paul's use as declaring Jesus divine, to be fully realised at the Second Coming. https://www.gotquestions.org/every-knee-shall-bow.html

**v. 24:**
- Ellicott: the prophet hears this confession spoken in the distant future. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-45.html
- The Pulpit Commentary renders it "all that *were* incensed," meaning God's former enemies will repent and be ashamed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/45.htm

**v. 25:**
- Ellicott sees an early form of the New Testament idea of union with God, being "in the Lord" or "in Christ." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/45.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary, following Cheyne: the whole "Israel of God" is justified by being joined to the LORD. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/45.htm

## 2. Where Protestant traditions differ

In what I could read, the traditions mostly agree. These are differences of emphasis, not open disagreements.

**v. 7:**
- **Reformed:** Calvin rejects "fanatics" who make God the author of sin. He keeps the distinction that God causes the evil of punishment but not of guilt. He adds that God doesn't inspire wicked people's malice but uses it to discipline his people, as he did with Pharaoh. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/45-7.html
- **Free-will emphasis:** Don Stewart (Blue Letter Bible) instead stresses that evil came from sin, which God didn't want, and that God gave people the ability to choose. https://www.blueletterbible.org/faq/don_stewart/don_stewart_1379.cfm

**v. 22 and 23:**
- **Baptist, Calvinist:** Gill says "every knee" means at least most of humanity coming to Christ when the full number of Gentiles comes in and the Jews are converted. He notes Paul applies it to the judgment day, when all must confess Christ "whether they will or not." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/45-23.htm
- **Baptist, Reformed:** John Piper says every tongue will confess "willingly or unwillingly," and that this will be owing finally to God, not to us. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-glory-of-christ
- Spurgeon, a Calvinist, preached the verse as an open invitation to all. He said "thou hast a perfect right to look," and that you are commanded to. https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/life-for-a-look

---

## 3. Other views

**Catholic (v. 7):** Catholic Answers says God can't do moral evil but can cause natural evil that serves good purposes. It reads the verse as being about natural evil, citing the Catholic RSV's "weal… woe." https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/did-god-create-evil

**Popular modern teaching (v. 18, the "gap theory"):** Chuck Smith notes that some use this verse to support the gap theory. That is the idea of an indefinite stretch of time between Genesis 1:1 and 1:2, since God says he didn't create the earth "without form." The excerpt didn't show his own verdict. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/45-18.html
